They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. etween $1 million and $1.5 million and the homes, more importantly, would need to be new construction.
While Proposition 37 has little opposition, and is supported by unions, chambers of commerce and organizations representing builders, the League of Women Voters opposes the ballot measure (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/), concerned it would saddle residents with too much debt and that the terms of these loans are opaque, the details worked out only after the vote.
New homes only
Only buyers of newly-built homes would be eligible for these loans. That could include existing commercial buildings that had been converted into homes, such as condos or townhomes.
This provision is uncommon as many existing down payment assistance programs don’t strictly limit the type of home someone can buy — only the sale price. Bob Hertzberg, former Senate Majority Leader and the architect of the proposal, said he wanted Proposition 37 to spur new construction.
“The problem is we have to increase supply,” Hertzberg said. The shortage of homes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-27/how-bad-is-californias-housing-shortage-it-depends-on-whos-doing-the-counting) in the state is estimated to range anywhere from 840,000 (https://upforgrowth.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/2024_Housing-Underproduction-in-the-U.S.-Report_Final-c-1.pdf) to upwards of 3 million. (https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/mckinsey/industries/public%20and%20social%20sector/our%20insights/closing%20californias%20housing%20gap/closing-californias-housing-gap-full-report.pdf)
Advertisement
By creating more demand for new homes, he said, the hope is that builders will respond en masse.
But some groups are wary of this logic. One analysis (https://voteyeson37.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Prop-37-Homeownership-Analysis-1.pdf), funded by the Proposition 37 campaign, estimated that this program could result in the building of 190,000 homes in the state, although the report’s author said it was “impossible to know” the true number given the various factors that impact housing.
Matthew Lewis, director of communications for California YIMBY, an organization that advocates making it easier and cheaper to build homes, said high prices make it clear that the demand for homes already exists and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
For Subscribers (https://www.latimes.com/topic/for-la-times-subscribers)
Why L.A. developers aren’t building more apartments, despite epic housing shortage (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-22/la-developers-arent-building-more-apartments-despite-epic-housing-shortage)
L.A. needs more multifamily housing, but developers say it doesn’t make sense to build apartments in the current market.
Sept. 22, 2026
“In concept, [Proposition 37 is] a great idea,” Lewis said. “The thing we’re concerned about is, California is still way behind on its housing production goals, so there’s the risk of an unintended consequence of instead of having 10 people bidding on a house, now you’ve given a couple folks down payment assistance, and so there’s now 12 people bidding on the same house.”
To drive builders to construct eligible homes, the measure would allow them to opt into a “qualified builder” option. As long as they adhere to price caps, agree to certain labor requirements and fix repairs that arise, they’re protected from lawsuits from buyers concerning defects 10 years after construction of the home.
Homebuilders say even given some relief from litigation, they aren’t sure Proposition 37 would push construction into overdrive.
Advertisement
“There are so many more things the state, city and county could do to help add more supply [of homes],” said Paul Schon, a developer who builds apartments in L.A. County. He said tackling permitting times and red tape involved in building would have a greater impact. “This is minor,” he said.
Interest rates could be a tough sell
Many down payment assistance programs offer interest-free loans to homebuyers, including an existing program run by CalHFA.
But in order to be self-funding, the fixed-rate loans offered through Proposition 37 would carry interest. If passed, the state would issue revenue bonds, selling them to investors and using that money to issue loans to homebuyers. The investors are repaid with the interest paid on the loans.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026), CalHFA would decide the total amount of bonds to issue and over what period of time.
Revenue bonds are generally viewed as riskier than other types of government bonds, in part because they’re backed by the promise of revenue from a specific project (https://www.msrb.org/Sources-Repayment) — in this case, payment by individual borrowers. That means interest rates on these loans could be higher than borrowers might like or be able to afford.
Hertzberg said he’s talked to investors who may be willing to buy these bonds at cheaper rates, given the crushing issue the funding is trying to solve. This would keep interest rates down for borrowers. He said he’s appealing to foundations and socially-minded tech leaders.
Advertisement
One of the biggest financial backers of the measure is the political nonprofit Building a Better California, which has been fighting the billionaire’s tax with help from wealthy donors (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax), including Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Hertzberg, for his part, refused to name any organization or person who may be interested in buying the bonds that would fund this program.

Prop. 37 explained: Can a $25 billion bond make homeownership in California attainable?
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)

In summary
A clever solution or a confusing gimmick? Like it or hate it, almost everyone has questions about Proposition 37. Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
It’s a bond, but not like any other bond on the ballot.
It promises to provide homebuyers with mortgages, but not your typical mortgages.
It would set up a down payment assistance program, but one unlike any other in the country.
There are plenty of consequential and controversial propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) on California’s ballot this year, but none as plainly weird as Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/).
Supporters call it an “elegant” solution to the fact that so many Californians can’t afford to buy a home. Detractors characterize it as a Rube Goldberg-esque gimmick (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/?clearUserState=true) that’s too clever by half. Virtually everyone, including some hired to analyze the proposition, has questions.
Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Q: What would Proposition 37 do?
A: If it passes, the state would be able to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a new loan program to help people afford down payments on new home purchases.
$25 billion ? With a “B”? That’s a lot of money, even for a state with a $352 billion budget (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-gavin-newsom-final-budget-deal/) .
It is. But unlike other bonds on the ballot, this isn’t supposed to cost the state anything.
When the state sells bonds, it’s borrowing money. Most bonds, like Propositions 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) and 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), would be paid back directly with tax dollars.
With Prop. 37, the state would act more like a loan broker. The California Housing Finance Agency would borrow the money from private lenders (by selling them bonds) and then re-lend that money to homebuyers. When the homebuyers repay those loans, the money would go back to the bond holders with interest.

If homebuyers don’t make their payments, the private lenders would be left holding the bag, not state taxpayers. That’s according to the text of the measure, anyway, though some analysts (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-37#:~:text=But%20a,period) have expressed doubt that state lawmakers could resist the political pressure to bail out homebuyers in the event of a wave of defaults.
Are these loans just home mortgages?
Second mortgages, specifically.
Buyers would still have to purchase a house the old fashioned way, by going to a bank or broker and taking out a mortgage that covers the bulk of the home price. But that still leaves a down payment. The median down payment in California is 20%, according to the California Association of Realtors — though it tends to be lower for first-time buyers. For an $800,000 home, that’s $160,000.
That’s a lot! Is this second mortgage meant to cover the entire down payment?
Almost all of it.
The program would allow these loans to cover as much as 17% of a home’s value, reducing the $160,000 to $24,000.
Is helping people take on more debt when they buy a home a good thing?
Homeownership is hopelessly out of reach for many Californians, even those who might otherwise be considered comfortably middle class. California has either the second-lowest (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/data/rates.html) or lowest (https://www.minneapolisfed.org/community-development-and-engagement/data-and-resources/homeowners-to-population-data) homeownership rate of any state, depending on how you measure it.
For many Californians stuck renting, high monthly mortgage payments — reliably higher (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/12/homeownership-vs-renting/) than a typical rent across much of the state — make homebuying a no-go. For anyone in that situation, tacking on a second mortgage with another monthly payment isn’t going to help.
But for some, it’s the size of the down payment that keeps homeownership out of reach. Roughly 40% of recent buyers turned to friends or family to help bridge this financial gap, according to a national survey (https://www.lendingtree.com/home/mortgage/down-payment-help-survey/#more-than-1-in-3-who-received-help-say-they-couldnt-have-bought-their-home-without-it). The gap is especially large in California, where home values are so high.
Asking a family to squirrel that much away is like asking them to “travel to the moon in a cardboard rocket ship,” Bob Hertzberg said in an interview.
Funny metaphor, but who is Bob Hertzberg?
He’s the former Speaker of the state Assembly, the former Senate majority leader, an active wheeler dealer in a wide variety of contemporary California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-forever-solano-shipyard-deal/#:~:text=former%20Senate%20Majority%20Leader%20Bob%20Hertzberg) political (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-10/measure-ula-bill#:~:text=Bob%20Hertzberg) debates and Prop. 37’s singularly energetic author and hypeman.
Hertzberg has been working on this idea for years, along with the California Association of Realtors, and he says he’s come up with an admittedly unusual, but very “elegant” solution for middle-class renters unable to scrounge together a down payment.
If this passes, would I be able to get one of these loans?
If you’re a typical Californian, it’s quite likely you’d at least be eligible.
Under this program, anyone making less than double their county’s typical income qualifies, which ranges from roughly $116,000 in Imperial to just over $410,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. That covers roughly 90% of all renters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37?utm_source=ppic&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=blog_subscriber), according to a recent Public Policy Institute of California analysis.
Hertzberg and other supporters think it’s a good thing that such a wide swath of California would qualify.
There are plenty of existing down payment assistance programs aimed at helping lower income (https://www.bankrate.com/mortgages/what-is-an-fha-loan/), first-generation (https://calmatters.org/california-divide/2024/01/dream-for-all-california/) or veteran (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) homebuyers, but Hertzberg argues that the broadly defined middle class needs help. Plus, the minimal qualifications will make it relatively light on red tape, he said.
But some opponents, like the League of Women Voters of California (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/), worry that offering a potential boost to so many would-be buyers will mean those who need help the least — people shy of the income cap, endowed with considerable wealth or able to borrow from family — will be the most likely to get the loans.
That, they warn, will only re-enforce the state’s existing economic and racial disparities (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/).
What kind of house could a borrower get with one of these second mortgages?
Two conditions apply.
First, there’s a price cap. This gets a little technical, but basically the home has to be less than about $1 million in inland California and up to $1.5 million in Los Angeles, Orange County and the Bay Area.
Second, the home has to be newly built or newly converted into housing. In other words, the borrower has to be its first occupant. No re-sales.

Why only new homes?
This gets at a common critique (https://www.aei.org/research-products/report/determining-the-price-impact-of-harris-down-payment-assistance-proposal/) of down payment assistance programs.
Giving some buyers a financial leg up without changing the number of units in circulation just shifts around who gets a house and who doesn’t. It’s like reserving a seat for someone during a game of musical chairs. Your friend might get a spot, but the same number of people will end up on the floor when the music stops.
Worst-case scenario, the new injection of money just pushes prices up further.
Reserving these loans for new units, the idea goes, would help ensure that new supply matches the new demand, resulting in a net increase in the number of homes and California homeowners.
How many homes would actually get built thanks to this program?
It could result in the construction of as many as 190,000 homes, according to an analysis (https://voteyeson37.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Prop-37-Homeownership-Analysis-1.pdf) commissioned by the Yes on 37 campaign. But the author concedes that’s at the high-end.
To encourage the industry to build eligible homes, the measure includes a “qualified builder” option. If a builder agrees to abide by the measure’s price cap and accept legal responsibility if they violate some basic labor requirements, they’re shielded from construction defect lawsuits as long as they repair any future mistakes to a homeowner’s satisfaction. When disputes end up in court anyway, legal fees would be capped.
The actual number of new units depends on how many builders decide it’s worth it to get qualified, how many of these homes would have been built anyway, the price of home and how much of the down payment each borrower wants to cover with the loan, along with a whole bunch of other unknowns.
What other unknowns?
There are quite a few, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026) highlighted two big ones in its analysis of the measure.
We don’t know whether investors would actually buy these bonds, and if so, at what rate. We also don’t know how many buyers will actually want to apply for these loans.
Why might bond buyers not want to lend the money?
Financing second mortgages is considered riskier than funding the traditional kind, because the loans add to a borrower’s debt load, the first loan is first in line to be paid back and the second wouldn’t come with the implicit guarantee of either the state of California or federal mortgage giants Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. If the borrower goes bust, the investor is on the hook.
Typical investors would want to be compensated for all that added risk. That means high interest rates.
Right now, traditional mortgage rates are blowing past 7% (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/25/business/interest-rates-economy-markets-inflation-mortgages.html). Ordinary investors “are going to want a fair amount more than that” for an untested, riskier investment, said Edward Pinto, who co-directs the Housing Center at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank.
Is this why buyers might not want to make use of these loans?
It’s the main reason.
Even if the second mortgage came with a 7% rate, that could add an extra $1,000 to a new homeowner’s monthly debt payments, depending on the price of the home. That’s a steep price to pay for a lower down payment. Less than 40% of Prop. 37-eligible renters would be able to afford these higher monthly payments for an entry-level home, according to the PPIC analysis (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37?utm_source=ppic&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=blog_subscriber).
For a house priced at the top of the eligibility range, less than half of one percent of eligible renters would be able to afford it.
Is there anything the state could do to bring these interest rates down?
Public money isn’t supposed to subsidize or backstop these loans, so not directly.
But Hertzberg said he has a plan.
Philanthropic groups and do-gooder foundations — “the Giving Pledge people,” in his words — might be convinced to purchase the bonds at below-market rates, potentially as low as 3%. This would be in the civic-minded spirit similar to buying war bonds during the Second World War, said Hertzberg. But it might also satisfy certain corporate social impact requirements, non-profit mission statements and even federal community lending standards (https://www.federalreserve.gov/consumerscommunities/cra_about.htm).
He said he’s already spoken to some possible donors about this, but has declined to name names.
So what happens if either investors don’t buy the bonds, buyers don’t take out the loans, or both?
Potentially nothing.
At a recent panel discussion (https://players.brightcove.net/876630612001/2eCBwdutJ_default/index.html?videoId=6406972609112), Chris Hoene, executive director of the left-leaning California Budget & Policy Center, said he was skeptical that Prop. 37 would work as advertised. But he also said the downside is limited.
“It could still work, and if it doesn’t work, the state’s not really on the hook,” he said.
So he doesn’t really like it, but said it can’t hurt? That’s weird.
I told you.
For the record: This story was corrected to note that Prop. 37 loans could be used to purchase any home sold under the policy’s specified price cap, even if the builder is not part of the “qualified builder” program.

Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. Below are lists of the top 10 contributors to committees that have raised at least $1,000,000 and are primarily formed to support or oppose a state ballot measure or a candidate for state office in the November 2026 General Election.
The lists do not show all contributions to every state ballot measure, or each independent expenditure committee formed to support or oppose a state candidate, only those committees that have raised $1,000,000 or more and have at least one contributor of $10,000 or more.
For itemized contribution and expenditure reports on state ballot measures, go to the CA Secretary of State's Ballot Measure (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Measures/).
For itemized contribution and expenditure reports on state candidates, go to the CA Secretary of State's Candidate (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Candidates/).
*A contributor whose name is marked with an asterisk made a contribution to a committee that simultaneously supported or opposed more than one potential ballot measure for the same election. Because of this, it is not possible to determine the amount of the contribution that was spent specifically on the campaign for any particular measure. In these cases, the contributions are listed for each ballot measure the committee has been formed to support or oppose. This results in the same contribution appearing multiple times - once for each ballot measure the committee supports or opposes.
The top 10 lists reflect the most recently available data. During the 90 days before an election, the FPPC makes every attempt to ensure that the lists are updated within one business day of receiving new information. Otherwise, the top contributor lists are updated weekly.

IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
California Middle Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 37 is a citizen-initiated state statute submitted to the California Attorney General’s Office on August 15, 2025. To qualify for the 2026 ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On April 21, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that enough valid signatures had been verified for the initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 37.
Proposition 37 would allow the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a new homebuyer assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Eligible buyers could receive a second mortgage covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, while providing at least a 3% down payment themselves. Eligibility would be limited based on residency, household income, home price, and other requirements. The measure would also give housing developers the option to follow higher labor standards in exchange for more flexible construction-defect rules.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 37 would have no direct costs to state or local governments because participating homebuyers would repay the bonds fully through their loan payments. The measure’s broader financial impact is uncertain and would depend on investor purchase of the bonds, the affordability of the loans compared with other programs, and whether the program increases home construction and homeownership.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports creating a state second-mortgage program to help eligible California homebuyers purchase a home, funded by up to $25 billion in bonds issued by the California Housing Finance Agency.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating the state second-mortgage homebuyer program.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 37 would make homeownership more attainable for middle-class and first-time buyers through low-interest down payment assistance with no cost to taxpayers. They also say it would encourage construction of new homes, increase the housing supply, create jobs, and help families build wealth through homeownership.
No argument against Proposition 37 was submitted for the official Voter Information Guide.

California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it.

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.

The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a chapter to the Health and Safety Code directing CalHFA to run a "Middle-Class Home Ownership Loan Program" and authorizing it to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, the kind repaid by the program's own income rather than by the state. Each loan "shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price" and must be secured by a second mortgage behind the buyer's primary loan. The agency has to launch the program within one year of the measure taking effect, and it decides how many bonds to sell and when, "in a manner that minimizes interest costs and encourages broad investor participation."
The repayment design is in section 51515.05. CalHFA sets the interest rates, amortization schedules and payment terms "on terms the agency determines practical and favorable to applicants and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds," plus "all costs of administration." The loans must be fixed-rate, the agency may let a borrower use the loan for closing costs if that "balances the interests of borrowers and bond investors," and every bond must state on its face that it "shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California." The program is restricted to new homes. A "qualified new home" is a newly built house, townhome, row house, condominium or manufactured home, or a unit in a former nonresidential building converted to housing, in either case "where the borrower is the first purchaser." Builders may sell qualified homes to anyone; only buyers using the loan must meet the program's rules. California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it.

Updated

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.

Each loan "shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price" and must be secured by a second mortgage behind the buyer's primary loan. The agency has to launch the program within one year of the measure taking effect, and it decides how many bonds to sell and when, "in a manner that minimizes interest costs and encourages broad investor participation."
The repayment design is in section 51515.05. CalHFA sets the interest rates, amortization schedules and payment terms "on terms the agency determines practical and favorable to applicants and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds," plus "all costs of administration." The loans must be fixed-rate, the agency may let a borrower use the loan for closing costs if that "balances the interests of borrowers and bond investors," and every bond must state on its face that it "shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California." The program is restricted to new homes. A "qualified new home" is a newly built house, townhome, row house, condominium or manufactured home, or a unit in a former nonresidential building converted to housing, in either case "where the borrower is the first purchaser." Builders may sell qualified homes to anyone; only buyers using the loan must meet the program's rules. California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it.

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.

This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. Each loan "shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price" and must be secured by a second mortgage behind the buyer's primary loan. The agency has to launch the program within one year of the measure taking effect, and it decides how many bonds to sell and when, "in a manner that minimizes interest costs and encourages broad investor participation."
The repayment design is in section 51515.05. CalHFA sets the interest rates, amortization schedules and payment terms "on terms the agency determines practical and favorable to applicants and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds," plus "all costs of administration." The loans must be fixed-rate, the agency may let a borrower use the loan for closing costs if that "balances the interests of borrowers and bond investors," and every bond must state on its face that it "shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California." The program is restricted to new homes. A "qualified new home" is a newly built house, townhome, row house, condominium or manufactured home, or a unit in a former nonresidential building converted to housing, in either case "where the borrower is the first purchaser." Builders may sell qualified homes to anyone; only buyers using the loan must meet the program's rules. Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
California Middle Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 37 is a citizen-initiated state statute submitted to the California Attorney General’s Office on August 15, 2025. To qualify for the 2026 ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On April 21, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that enough valid signatures had been verified for the initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 37.
Proposition 37 would allow the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a new homebuyer assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Eligible buyers could receive a second mortgage covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, while providing at least a 3% down payment themselves. Eligibility would be limited based on residency, household income, home price, and other requirements. The measure would also give housing developers the option to follow higher labor standards in exchange for more flexible construction-defect rules.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 37 would have no direct costs to state or local governments because participating homebuyers would repay the bonds fully through their loan payments. The measure’s broader financial impact is uncertain and would depend on investor purchase of the bonds, the affordability of the loans compared with other programs, and whether the program increases home construction and homeownership.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports creating a state second-mortgage program to help eligible California homebuyers purchase a home, funded by up to $25 billion in bonds issued by the California Housing Finance Agency.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating the state second-mortgage homebuyer program.

Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
California Middle Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 37 is a citizen-initiated state statute submitted to the California Attorney General’s Office on August 15, 2025. To qualify for the 2026 ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On April 21, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that enough valid signatures had been verified for the initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 37.
Proposition 37 would allow the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a new homebuyer assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Eligible buyers could receive a second mortgage covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, while providing at least a 3% down payment themselves. Eligibility would be limited based on residency, household income, home price, and other requirements. The measure would also give housing developers the option to follow higher labor standards in exchange for more flexible construction-defect rules.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 37 would have no direct costs to state or local governments because participating homebuyers would repay the bonds fully through their loan payments. The measure’s broader financial impact is uncertain and would depend on investor purchase of the bonds, the affordability of the loans compared with other programs, and whether the program increases home construction and homeownership.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports creating a state second-mortgage program to help eligible California homebuyers purchase a home, funded by up to $25 billion in bonds issued by the California Housing Finance Agency.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating the state second-mortgage homebuyer program.

November 2026 General Election
Last Modified: October 30, 2026
Below are lists of the top 10 contributors to committees that have raised at least $1,000,000 and are primarily formed to support or oppose a state ballot measure or a candidate for state office in the November 2026 General Election.
The lists do not show all contributions to every state ballot measure, or each independent expenditure committee formed to support or oppose a state candidate, only those committees that have raised $1,000,000 or more and have at least one contributor of $10,000 or more.
For itemized contribution and expenditure reports on state ballot measures, go to the CA Secretary of State's Ballot Measure (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Measures/).
For itemized contribution and expenditure reports on state candidates, go to the CA Secretary of State's Candidate (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Candidates/).
*A contributor whose name is marked with an asterisk made a contribution to a committee that simultaneously supported or opposed more than one potential ballot measure for the same election. Because of this, it is not possible to determine the amount of the contribution that was spent specifically on the campaign for any particular measure. In these cases, the contributions are listed for each ballot measure the committee has been formed to support or oppose. This results in the same contribution appearing multiple times - once for each ballot measure the committee supports or opposes.
The top 10 lists reflect the most recently available data. During the 90 days before an election, the FPPC makes every attempt to ensure that the lists are updated within one business day of receiving new information. Otherwise, the top contributor lists are updated weekly.

November 2026 General Election
Last Modified: October 30, 2026
Below are lists of the top 10 contributors to committees that have raised at least $1,000,000 and are primarily formed to support or oppose a state ballot measure or a candidate for state office in the November 2026 General Election.
The lists do not show all contributions to every state ballot measure, or each independent expenditure committee formed to support or oppose a state candidate, only those committees that have raised $1,000,000 or more and have at least one contributor of $10,000 or more.
For itemized contribution and expenditure reports on state ballot measures, go to the CA Secretary of State's Ballot Measure (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Measures/).
For itemized contribution and expenditure reports on state candidates, go to the CA Secretary of State's Candidate (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Candidates/).
*A contributor whose name is marked with an asterisk made a contribution to a committee that simultaneously supported or opposed more than one potential ballot measure for the same election. Because of this, it is not possible to determine the amount of the contribution that was spent specifically on the campaign for any particular measure. In these cases, the contributions are listed for each ballot measure the committee has been formed to support or oppose. This results in the same contribution appearing multiple times - once for each ballot measure the committee supports or opposes.
The top 10 lists reflect the most recently available data. During the 90 days before an election, the FPPC makes every attempt to ensure that the lists are updated within one business day of receiving new information. Otherwise, the top contributor lists are updated weekly.

California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it.

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.

Each loan "shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price" and must be secured by a second mortgage behind the buyer's primary loan. The agency has to launch the program within one year of the measure taking effect, and it decides how many bonds to sell and when, "in a manner that minimizes interest costs and encourages broad investor participation."
The repayment design is in section 51515.05. CalHFA sets the interest rates, amortization schedules and payment terms "on terms the agency determines practical and favorable to applicants and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds," plus "all costs of administration." The loans must be fixed-rate, the agency may let a borrower use the loan for closing costs if that "balances the interests of borrowers and bond investors," and every bond must state on its face that it "shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California." The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm) notes that CalHFA "also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible," and that the measure leaves the rate itself to the agency.
The program is restricted to new homes. A "qualified new home" is a newly built house, townhome, row house, condominium or manufactured home, or a unit in a former nonresidential building converted to housing, in either case "where the borrower is the first purchaser." Builders may sell qualified homes to anyone; only buyers using the loan must meet the program's rules. Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
California Middle Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 37 is a citizen-initiated state statute submitted to the California Attorney General’s Office on August 15, 2025. To qualify for the 2026 ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On April 21, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that enough valid signatures had been verified for the initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 37.
Proposition 37 would allow the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a new homebuyer assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Eligible buyers could receive a second mortgage covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, while providing at least a 3% down payment themselves. Eligibility would be limited based on residency, household income, home price, and other requirements. The measure would also give housing developers the option to follow higher labor standards in exchange for more flexible construction-defect rules.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 37 would have no direct costs to state or local governments because participating homebuyers would repay the bonds fully through their loan payments. The measure’s broader financial impact is uncertain and would depend on investor purchase of the bonds, the affordability of the loans compared with other programs, and whether the program increases home construction and homeownership.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports creating a state second-mortgage program to help eligible California homebuyers purchase a home, funded by up to $25 billion in bonds issued by the California Housing Finance Agency.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating the state second-mortgage homebuyer program.

Below are lists of the top 10 contributors to committees that have raised at least $1,000,000 and are primarily formed to support or oppose a state ballot measure or a candidate for state office in the November 2026 General Election.
The lists do not show all contributions to every state ballot measure, or each independent expenditure committee formed to support or oppose a state candidate, only those committees that have raised $1,000,000 or more and have at least one contributor of $10,000 or more.
For itemized contribution and expenditure reports on state ballot measures, go to the CA Secretary of State's Ballot Measure (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Measures/).
For itemized contribution and expenditure reports on state candidates, go to the CA Secretary of State's Candidate (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Candidates/).
*A contributor whose name is marked with an asterisk made a contribution to a committee that simultaneously supported or opposed more than one potential ballot measure for the same election. Because of this, it is not possible to determine the amount of the contribution that was spent specifically on the campaign for any particular measure. In these cases, the contributions are listed for each ballot measure the committee has been formed to support or oppose. This results in the same contribution appearing multiple times - once for each ballot measure the committee supports or opposes.

assistantMessageEvent.delta:
**Analyzing Proposition 37**

Okay, I've got the basics down on California's Proposition 37, which is slated for the November 3, 2026 General Election. Specifically, this proposition seems to be creating a loan program for middle-income buyers of certain new homes. That's a solid initial framework to start with, I think.

**Examining Loan Details**

I'm now diving deeper into the specifics of the loan program. It seems CalHFA will issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to provide fixed-rate second mortgages. Repayment comes from homeowners' mortgage payments, with the Legislative Analyst's Office stating no direct state or local costs. This proposition also requires a simple majority to pass.

**Assessing Public Sentiment**

I've been reviewing the polling data, and the trends are quite clear. The PPIC survey in October shows a significant lead for the "Yes" side, with 65% support. The AIMSA survey confirms this strong "Yes" sentiment, with 59%. Both polls indicate a clear path for Proposition 37's passage. I'm seeing no significant obstacles or changing dynamics that would suggest any other outcome.

37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Zero Taxpayer Cost-No Taxpayer Risk. Prop. 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, NOT TAXPAYERS. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
FOR

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
State Revenue Bonds. Bonds are a way that governments borrow money, most commonly for public projects such as schools or bridges. The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects. Over time, investors are repaid with interest. The state sells two main types of bonds: general obligation bonds and revenue bonds. The state usually repays general obligation bonds using the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) In contrast, revenue bonds are repaid using revenue from fees or other payments by the users of the project (such as from bridge tolls).
Some People Seek Down Payment Assistance. When purchasing a home, most people pay some of the cost up front-typically 3 percent to 20 percent of the home price. The up-front payment is known as a down payment. If people cannot afford the down payment, there are different government programs available to provide down payment assistance to eligible homebuyers. To cover the remaining cost of the home, homebuyers get a loan, called a mortgage. Homebuyers then pay off the mortgage by making monthly payments that include interest.
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). CalHFA is a state entity that administers programs designed to help low- and moderate-income Californians afford housing. CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.
Construction Defect Law. To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction. Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards. For example, the homeowner must provide notice to the builder that includes certain information concerning a claim of construction defect.
PROPOSAL
Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program. Proposition 37 allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. CalHFA would use the bond funds to create a down payment assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Each loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home price. (Homebuyers would need to provide a down payment of at least 3 percent of the home price.) Homeowners’ monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program’s administrative costs. CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible. CalHFA would decide how much of the bonds to issue (up to $25 billion) and over what time period.
Buyers and Homes Must Meet Certain Requirements. To participate in a middleclass homeownership loan, people and homes would need to meet certain requirements. For example, an applicant would need to be a resident of the state and have a household income no more than double the typical income level in their area. For a home to be eligible for purchase through the program, among other requirements, the buyer would need to be the first purchaser of the home and the price could not exceed certain limits.
Housing Developer Options. Under Proposition 37, all developers could build homes eligible for purchase under the program. Developers also could choose to participate in a “qualified builder option.” Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects. In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.
FISCAL EFFECTS
No Direct State or Local Costs. Because Proposition 37 uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs.
Other Potential Effects. A number of factors, which are unknown at this time, could affect Proposition 37’s scope and impact. These include (1) the extent to which investors want to buy the bond, (2) how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options, and (3) whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying.

CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 37
VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 37: the California Middle- Class Homeownership & Family Home Construction Act. Proposition 37 creates affordable homeownership opportunities for working and middle-class Californians and encourages new home construction-with ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS.
California has the second-worst homeownership rate in the nation; rising costs push homeownership further out of reach every year.
With the statewide median home price now exceeding $930,000, a traditional 20% down payment can require saving over $186,000 just to get in the door. Teachers, nurses, veterans, and firefighters work hard and pay their bills. They can afford monthly mortgage payments but are locked out of homeownership in the communities where they live and work because down payment requirements are too high.
Proposition 37 gives working and middle-class Californians a fair shot at homeownership.
KEEPING HOMEOWNERSHIP WITHIN REACH.
Prop. 37 is a practical solution. It makes consumer-friendly, low-interest downpayment assistance loans available to qualified California residents for purchasing a newly built home, with no cost to taxpayers.
This is not a handout. Homebuyers must qualify for a mortgage, meet income requirements, pay at least 3% down, occupy the home as their primary residence, make monthly payments, and fully repay their loans.
Prop. 37 is designed for renters, first-time homebuyers, and working families who earn too much to qualify for renter assistance programs, but not enough to save the massive down payment required to buy a home.
“Proposition 37 will boost homeownership without burdening taxpayers. As a state revenue bond, downpayment assistance loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers, not taxpayers.” -Malia Cohen, California State Controller
BUILDS MORE HOMES, CREATES GOOD JOBS.
California hasn’t built enough homes to keep up with demand. By helping qualified buyers purchase newly built homes, Prop. 37 will help accelerate construction, creating thousands of good-paying jobs and generating economic investment.
Expanding the housing supply helps workers and families to stay in California, build equity, raise their children, and live in the communities where they work.
ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS.
Taxpayer advocates and California’s Legislative Analyst agree: Proposition 37 has no cost to taxpayers. Loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers-not taxpayers.
STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND CONSUMER PROTECTIONS.
Prop. 37 includes fiscal accountability and transparency requirements, construction accountability standards, and annual audits detailing the status of loans made and the fund’s financial condition.
Consumer benefits include below-market, fixed-rate loans, protections from unfair lending practices, strict limits on lender fees, and no penalty for early repayment.
BROAD, BIPARTISAN SUPPORT
Proposition 37 is supported by Democrats & Republicans, labor and businesses, construction workers, taxpayer and housing advocates, veterans, the California Teachers Association, and United Nurses Association of California.
For generations, homeownership provided stability, security, and a path to the middle class. But today, that path is simply out of reach for too many Californians. Proposition 37 is a practical solution that tackles one of the biggest barriers to homeownership, without burdening taxpayers.
Vote YES to expand middle-class homeownership, build more homes, create good jobs, and give working Californians a fair chance to live, work, raise a family, and stay in California.
VoteYeson37.com
Danny Curtin , Director
California Conference of Carpenters
Fiona Ma , Boardmember
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA)

California State Commanders Veterans Council
